Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
33-year-old woman with first-episode, sudden-onset unilateral headache accompanied by visual aura, nausea, and vomiting—clinical picture most consistent with migraine with aura; safety-net advice and same-day in-person review arranged.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Left-sided headache started abruptly ~4 h ago.  
• Course/severity: Immediate onset, rated 6/10; worsens with movement; unrelieved by paracetamol taken 3 h ago.  
• Associated symptoms: Blurred vision with zig-zag lines, dizziness, photophobia (cannot tolerate screens), two episodes of vomiting, ongoing nausea.  
• Pertinent negatives: No limb weakness, gait disturbance, speech difficulty, neck stiffness, fever, or prior similar headaches.  
• PMH: Kidney stones; no previous migraines.  
• FHx: Mother—migraine and hypothyroidism.  
• Medications: None (took paracetamol today).  
• Allergies: Denies known drug allergies.  
• Social/OB: Denies likelihood of pregnancy. No other social history discussed. Preventive care not covered.

Examination:
• Tele-consultation; no vitals provided.  
• Patient alert, coherent; reports normal gait. No focal neurological deficits elicited. No other physical findings documented.

Impression:
Likely migraine with aura  
– Supporting: Unilateral headache, visual zig-zag aura, nausea/vomiting, photophobia, family history, absence of focal deficits.  
Alternate considerations:  
1. Subarachnoid hemorrhage – sudden onset “first” headache; lower severity and lack of neuro signs make less likely but not excluded.  
2. Carotid/vertebral artery dissection – unilateral pain and visual change; low suspicion without neck pain/trauma or deficits.

Plan:
• Pharmacologic: Trial ibuprofen plus over-the-counter anti-emetic; encourage oral hydration with sugary carbonated drink (e.g., cola).  
• Escalation: If inadequate relief, escalate to specific migraine therapies per step-wise ladder.  
• Follow-up: Same-day face-to-face appointment for full neurological examination; patient to cancel if fully recovered.  
• Safety-net: Seek urgent care (A&E) for worsening headache, new neurological symptoms, persistent vomiting, or if pain not improving within expected timeframe.  
• No prescriptions issued during call; advised on OTC options.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: Vitals, full neurological and fundoscopic examination, detailed medication and social history, documentation of pregnancy test if concern persists.  
● Conflicts: None significant between transcript and DDx (both support migraine as most likely).  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; occasional connection drop and minor overlaps but adequate for key clinical data.
